planting.note: Scatter seed on bare, disturbed soil in fall or winter and let winter rains trigger germination; avoid summer water entirely once seedlings establish.

directions: An intensely aromatic California annual with vivid violet-blue flowers and the genus's signature exaggerated curling stamens, this plant blooms heavily in late summer when little else is flowering in dry gardens, a major late-season nectar source for native bees and honeybees. It wants the leanest, driest, most neglected corner of the garden — hard clay or decomposed granite in full baking sun suits it far better than amended beds, since drought stress concentrates its pungent, vinegar-scented oils and intensifies bloom. It can be allelopathic to neighboring seedlings, so keep it apart from prized companions.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring on a slope or berm with sharp drainage so winter rain never pools at the crown; shear lightly after bloom to keep the shrub dense.

directions: A true woody chaparral shrub, unlike most of the genus, this bluecurls carries narrow aromatic leaves and showy blue flower spikes through spring and summer, giving long structural presence in a dry garden rather than a single annual flush. Treat it exactly like a small manzanita or ceanothus, resisting the urge to feed or water it once past its first summer. Because it tolerates both high-elevation chaparral exposure and coastal sage scrub heat, it bridges foothill gardens too hot and exposed for woolly blue curls.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or winter to catch rains into the hottest, driest spot available; source seed only from reputable native-seed suppliers given its watch-listed status.

directions: A true San Joaquin Valley endemic annual that blooms through the hottest part of summer into fall when most California natives have gone dormant, this bluecurls is valuable for Central Valley heat-garden and grassland-restoration palettes. A reclaimed alkaline or disturbed-soil patch mimics its native grassland niche better than a conventional bed. It is one of the few bluecurls that genuinely thrives through valley summer heat, making it a useful filler for interior-California meadow gardens that need color after spring annuals fade.

planting.note: Sow directly on bare sandy or sandhill-type soil in spring; avoid any soil enrichment, which produces weak, floppy stems and fewer flowers.

directions: This bluecurls fills the late-fall pollinator gap in eastern and southeastern gardens, blooming August through November when it's a favorite late-season forage plant for native bees, with a low, airy habit and fine-textured foliage suiting sandy, lean meadow plantings across a wide range from Alabama to New York. Its much later bloom window makes it worth pairing alongside the already-present forked bluecurls to extend the native-bee nectar season into November. It is well suited to pine-barren and longleaf-pine-understory restoration plantings.

planting.note: Sow on disturbed, unamended gravel or sand with good light; needs no summer irrigation and self-seeds in place.

directions: This bluecurls' affinity for serpentine and gravelly streambank soils makes it an excellent choice for the rocky, nutrient-poor problem areas of a foothill garden that defeat most other flowering annuals. Its strong turpentine-scented foliage deters browsing deer. Because its native range extends further north and higher in elevation than the rest of the genus, it is the bluecurls most likely to succeed in Sierra foothill and southern Cascade gardens where coastal chaparral species struggle with winter cold.
